chapter_text:
CHAPTER 9 — PHYSIOGRAPHY OF INDIA

Introduction

India is the seventh-largest country in the world by area (about 3.28 million sq km) and the most populous. From the snow-clad peaks of the Himalayas in the north to the tropical coasts of the south, India contains an extraordinary variety of physical landscapes. This chapter studies that PHYSIOGRAPHY — the physical features of the land — and groups it into six broad divisions:

  (1) The Himalayan mountains
  (2) The Northern Plains
  (3) The Peninsular Plateau
  (4) The Indian Desert
  (5) The Coastal Plains
  (6) The Islands

Understanding physiography is essential because it shapes climate, soils, vegetation, agriculture, population distribution and even history.

9.1 LOCATION AND EXTENT

India lies in the NORTHERN and EASTERN hemispheres between latitudes 8°4'N (Kanyakumari) and 37°6'N (in Jammu & Kashmir), and longitudes 68°7'E (in Gujarat) and 97°25'E (in Arunachal Pradesh). The TROPIC OF CANCER (23½°N) passes through the middle of the country — through Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram. The country is roughly 3214 km from north to south and 2933 km from east to west. India shares LAND BORDERS with Pakistan, Afghanistan (across PoK), China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar. To the south lie the INDIAN OCEAN, the ARABIAN SEA and the BAY OF BENGAL. Sri Lanka lies off the south-east coast, separated by the Palk Strait and the Gulf of Mannar.

9.2 THE HIMALAYAN MOUNTAINS

The HIMALAYAS (literally 'abode of snow') form a great arc some 2400 km long across India's northern border, from the Indus in the west to the Brahmaputra in the east. They are YOUNG FOLD MOUNTAINS, formed by the collision of the Indian plate with the Eurasian plate beginning ~50 million years ago, and they are still rising. The Himalayas contain the world's highest peaks — Mount Everest (8848 m, in Nepal) and India's tallest, Kangchenjunga (8586 m, in Sikkim).

The Himalayas have THREE longitudinal ranges:
 - HIMADRI (Greater Himalayas) — the northernmost, highest range; average elevation above 6000 m; always snow-clad; contains Everest, Kangchenjunga, Nanga Parbat.
 - HIMACHAL (Lesser Himalayas) — south of Himadri; elevations 3700-4500 m; contains the famous hill stations — Shimla, Mussoorie, Nainital, Darjeeling.
 - SHIVALIKS (Outer Himalayas) — southernmost; elevations 900-1100 m; composed of recent sediments; contain DUNS (longitudinal valleys, e.g. Dehradun, Patli Dun).

The Himalayas are also divided LONGITUDINALLY (west to east) into four regions:
 - PUNJAB Himalaya (Indus to Sutlej) — also called Kashmir Himalaya.
 - KUMAON Himalaya (Sutlej to Kali) — in Uttarakhand.
 - NEPAL Himalaya (Kali to Tista) — mostly in Nepal.
 - ASSAM Himalaya (Tista to Brahmaputra) — in Sikkim, Bhutan, Arunachal Pradesh.

The Himalayas are India's GREAT NATURAL BARRIER, source of perennial rivers, climate modifier, region of biodiversity, and cradle of unique cultures.

9.3 THE NORTHERN PLAINS

South of the Himalayas lie the NORTHERN PLAINS, formed by the alluvium deposited by three great rivers — the INDUS, the GANGA and the BRAHMAPUTRA — over millions of years. They stretch about 2400 km from west to east and are 240-320 km wide. They are extraordinarily flat (less than 1 m fall per km) and extremely fertile. The plains support nearly half of India's population.

Subdivisions of the plains, from north to south:
 - BHABAR — narrow belt at the foot of the Shivaliks where streams disappear into pebbles and boulders.
 - TARAI — marshy, forested belt south of Bhabar where streams reappear.
 - BHANGAR — older alluvium forming higher terraces, often containing kankar (calcareous nodules).
 - KHADAR — newer alluvium of the active flood plain, very fertile and renewed each year by floods.

The plains are divided regionally into:
 - PUNJAB-HARYANA plain — drained by the Indus tributaries (Beas, Sutlej etc.).
 - GANGA plain — the largest, from Delhi to West Bengal.
 - BRAHMAPUTRA valley — in Assam.

9.4 THE PENINSULAR PLATEAU

South of the Northern Plains lies the PENINSULAR PLATEAU — one of the OLDEST landmasses on Earth, made of ancient hard igneous and metamorphic rocks. It is roughly triangular, with the apex at Kanyakumari and the base running between the Aravalli and the Rajmahal hills. It is divided into:

 - CENTRAL HIGHLANDS — north of the Narmada river. Includes the Aravalli range (one of the oldest fold ranges in the world, now eroded), the Vindhya range, the Satpura range, and the Malwa plateau.
 - DECCAN PLATEAU — south of the Narmada. Triangular, bordered by the WESTERN GHATS in the west and the EASTERN GHATS in the east. The two Ghats meet in the south at the NILGIRI hills.
   * WESTERN GHATS: continuous, 900-1600 m high, steep western slope; contain Anaimudi (2695 m, the highest peak in peninsular India). They block south-west monsoon winds.
   * EASTERN GHATS: discontinuous, lower (~600 m), broken by rivers Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri.
 - The DECCAN LAVA (Deccan Traps) — vast layers of basaltic lava in western and central Deccan, erupted ~65 million years ago.

The Plateau is rich in MINERALS — iron, coal, manganese, bauxite, mica — and has been the site of major Indian dynasties.

9.5 THE INDIAN DESERT

West of the Aravallis lies the THAR DESERT — an arid region of sand dunes, rocky outcrops and salt lakes (Sambhar, Pachpadra). Annual rainfall is below 150 mm. The only large river is the LUNI, which flows into the Rann of Kachchh. The Thar covers most of western Rajasthan and parts of Gujarat. Despite the harsh climate, the desert has supported pastoral and oasis communities for centuries and is famous for its forts (Jaisalmer) and crafts.

9.6 THE COASTAL PLAINS

India has two coastal plains flanking the Peninsular Plateau:
 - WESTERN COASTAL PLAIN — narrow (50-100 km wide) between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea. From north to south it is divided into the KONKAN coast (Maharashtra), KANARA coast (Karnataka) and MALABAR coast (Kerala — famous for backwaters / lagoons).
 - EASTERN COASTAL PLAIN — wider (100-130 km), between the Eastern Ghats and the Bay of Bengal. From north to south: NORTHERN CIRCAR (Odisha to north Andhra Pradesh) and COROMANDEL coast (Tamil Nadu).

The eastern coast is associated with broad DELTAS of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri rivers. The western coast has few rivers reaching the sea but excellent natural HARBOURS (Mumbai, Marmagao, Mangalore, Kochi).

9.7 THE ISLANDS

India has two major island groups:
 - ANDAMAN AND NICOBAR ISLANDS — in the Bay of Bengal; 572 islands, mostly forested and volcanic in origin; Barren Island has India's only active volcano. Andamans are inhabited by indigenous tribes including the Sentinelese, the Onge and the Jarawa. Capital: Port Blair.
 - LAKSHADWEEP — in the Arabian Sea; coral islands (atolls); only about 10 are inhabited. Capital: Kavaratti.

SUMMARY

- India lies between 8°4'N and 37°6'N latitudes, with the Tropic of Cancer passing through its middle.
- It is geographically divided into six physiographic regions: the Himalayas, the Northern Plains, the Peninsular Plateau, the Indian Desert, the Coastal Plains, and the Islands.
- The Himalayas — young fold mountains in three parallel ranges (Himadri, Himachal, Shivalik) — form India's northern barrier and source of perennial rivers.
- The Northern Plains, formed by Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra alluvium, are extremely fertile and densely populated.
- The Peninsular Plateau is one of the oldest landmasses on Earth; the Western Ghats are continuous while the Eastern Ghats are broken by rivers.
- The Thar Desert lies in the west; the Coastal Plains lie east and west of the Peninsular Plateau; the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep are India's two island groups.

Outline the structure of the Northern Plains and identify their subdivisions (Bhabar, Tarai, Bhangar, Khadar).
Describe the divisions of the Peninsular Plateau, the Western and Eastern Ghats, and identify the importance of the Deccan Traps.
Identify the location, climate and physical features of the Thar Desert.
Describe the western and eastern coastal plains and the Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep island groups.
Distinguish between the Western and Eastern Ghats in terms of continuity, height and influence on climate.
Explain why the Himalayas are called a 'natural barrier' and discuss their role as climate modifier, water source and biodiversity reservoir.

chapter_summary.title: Physiography of India — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Social Science (213) summary for Lesson 9. India contains a remarkable variety of physical landscapes, grouped by physiographers into six divisions: the Himalayan mountains, the Northern Plains, the Peninsular Plateau, the Indian Desert (Thar), the Coastal Plains and the Islands. Each has distinctive geology, climate and human geography.

sections.heading: Location and extent
bullets: India lies between 8°4'N (Kanyakumari) and 37°6'N (J&K) latitudes, and between 68°7'E (Gujarat) and 97°25'E (Arunachal Pradesh) longitudes.
The Tropic of Cancer (23½°N) passes through eight Indian states roughly through the middle of the country.
India is the seventh largest country in the world by area (~3.28 million sq km) and shares borders with Pakistan, Afghanistan (PoK), China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar.
Indian Ocean lies to the south, Arabian Sea to the west and Bay of Bengal to the east.

sections.heading: The Himalayan mountains
bullets: The Himalayas are young fold mountains formed by the collision of the Indian plate with the Eurasian plate; they are still rising.
They stretch ~2400 km from the Indus in the west to the Brahmaputra in the east.
Three parallel longitudinal ranges: HIMADRI (Greater, highest, snow-clad; >6000 m); HIMACHAL (Lesser; hill stations); SHIVALIK (Outer; lowest, recent sediments, contains duns).
Four longitudinal regions: Punjab Himalaya, Kumaon Himalaya, Nepal Himalaya, Assam Himalaya.
Importance: form India's northern natural barrier; source of perennial rivers; modify climate; reservoir of biodiversity.

sections.heading: The Northern Plains
bullets: Formed by the alluvium of the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra rivers; about 2400 km west-east, 240-320 km north-south.
Very flat (less than 1 m fall per km) and very fertile; support nearly half of India's population.
Subdivisions north to south: BHABAR (narrow pebbly belt at the foot of Shivaliks), TARAI (marshy belt), BHANGAR (older alluvium), KHADAR (newer alluvium of active flood plain).
Three regional plains: Punjab-Haryana, Ganga, Brahmaputra valley.

sections.heading: The Peninsular Plateau
bullets: One of the oldest landmasses on Earth; hard igneous and metamorphic rocks.
Roughly triangular, with its apex at Kanyakumari and its base between Aravalli and Rajmahal hills.
Two main parts: CENTRAL HIGHLANDS (north of Narmada; Aravalli, Vindhya, Satpura, Malwa) and DECCAN PLATEAU (south of Narmada).
Bordered by the WESTERN GHATS (continuous, higher, ~900-1600 m) and the EASTERN GHATS (discontinuous, lower, broken by rivers).
Rich in minerals — iron, coal, manganese, bauxite, mica.

sections.heading: Desert, coasts and islands
bullets: The THAR Desert lies west of the Aravallis in Rajasthan and Gujarat; arid (<150 mm rainfall); only major river is the Luni.
WESTERN coastal plain (Konkan, Kanara, Malabar) is narrow with no major deltas but excellent harbours.
EASTERN coastal plain is wider with major DELTAS of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri.
ANDAMAN AND NICOBAR ISLANDS in the Bay of Bengal — volcanic in origin; 572 islands; Port Blair is capital.
LAKSHADWEEP in the Arabian Sea — coral atolls; Kavaratti is capital.

key_takeaways: India has six broad physiographic divisions: Himalayan mountains, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Indian Desert, Coastal Plains and Islands.
The Himalayas are young fold mountains arranged in three parallel ranges and four longitudinal regions.
The Northern Plains, formed of alluvium from three great rivers, are India's most fertile and densely populated region.
The Peninsular Plateau is one of the oldest landmasses on Earth, rich in minerals, with the continuous Western Ghats and discontinuous Eastern Ghats as borders.
Western coastal plain is narrow with good harbours; eastern coastal plain is wider with broad river deltas.
India has two island groups — Andaman & Nicobar in the Bay of Bengal and Lakshadweep in the Arabian Sea.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Physiography of India
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Use proper geographical terms and cite latitudes / longitudes where appropriate.

questions.question: State India's latitudinal and longitudinal extent.
questions.answer: India lies between latitudes 8°4'N (Kanyakumari) and 37°6'N (in Jammu & Kashmir), and between longitudes 68°7'E (in Gujarat) and 97°25'E (in Arunachal Pradesh). The country is about 3214 km from north to south and 2933 km from east to west.

questions.question: What is the Tropic of Cancer? Through which Indian states does it pass?
questions.answer: The Tropic of Cancer is the parallel of latitude at 23½° NORTH of the equator. It marks the northernmost latitude at which the sun can be directly overhead. In India, it passes through EIGHT states (west to east): GUJARAT, RAJASTHAN, MADHYA PRADESH, CHHATTISGARH, JHARKHAND, WEST BENGAL, TRIPURA and MIZORAM. Roughly, it divides India into a sub-tropical northern half and a tropical southern half.

questions.question: Name the three parallel ranges of the Himalayas in order from north to south.
questions.answer: From north to south: (1) HIMADRI (Greater Himalayas) — northernmost, highest, average above 6000 m, permanently snow-covered; contains Everest, Kangchenjunga. (2) HIMACHAL (Lesser Himalayas) — south of Himadri; 3700-4500 m; contains the famous hill stations. (3) SHIVALIK (Outer Himalayas) — southernmost, lowest, 900-1100 m; composed of recent sediments; contains the Duns (longitudinal valleys).

questions.question: What is a 'Dun'? Give two examples.
questions.answer: A DUN is a longitudinal valley lying between the Lesser Himalayas (Himachal) and the Outer Himalayas (Shivaliks). Duns are formed when the rising mountains created enclosed valleys later filled by river sediments. They are flat, fertile and well populated. Examples: DEHRADUN (in Uttarakhand — the largest dun) and PATLI DUN (further east). Other duns: Kotli Dun, Kothri Dun, Chumbi Dun.

questions.question: Why are the Northern Plains so fertile and densely populated?
questions.answer: The Northern Plains have several advantages that explain both their fertility and dense population. (1) FORMATION — they are made of ALLUVIUM deposited over millions of years by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra rivers. Alluvial soil is naturally rich in plant nutrients. (2) FLATNESS — the plains are extremely flat (less than 1 m fall per km), making them easy to till and irrigate. (3) WATER — perennial rivers and shallow water tables ensure year-round water supply. (4) CLIMATE — receive enough monsoon rainfall for two or even three crops a year. (5) CULTIVABILITY — the Khadar tracts are renewed yearly by river floods. Together these make the plains the most productive agricultural region in India — and have supported dense populations for thousands of years.

questions.question: Distinguish between Bhangar and Khadar.
questions.answer:
Both are subdivisions of the Northern Plains made of alluvium, but they differ in age and characteristics:

  BHANGAR — OLDER alluvium. Forms higher terraces and ground above the flood plain. Often contains KANKAR (calcareous nodules). Less fertile than Khadar but no flood risk.

  KHADAR — NEWER alluvium of the active FLOOD PLAIN. Lower in elevation. Renewed each year by flooding, so very fertile and free of kankar. Vulnerable to floods.

In many regions farmers grow rice and water-intensive crops on khadar and wheat / other crops on bhangar.

questions.question: Why is the Peninsular Plateau considered one of the oldest landmasses on Earth?
questions.answer: Because it is made of very ancient (mostly PRE-CAMBRIAN) IGNEOUS and METAMORPHIC rocks — granites and gneisses — that have been in place for billions of years. Unlike the young, still-rising Himalayas, the Peninsular Plateau has been STABLE for hundreds of millions of years. It was once part of the supercontinent GONDWANALAND, which broke apart ~140 million years ago. The plateau drifted north on the Indian Plate and eventually collided with Eurasia to throw up the Himalayas — but the plateau itself remained as the ancient core of India.

questions.question: Compare the Western Ghats with the Eastern Ghats.
questions.answer:

  Continuity        Continuous, unbroken                   Discontinuous, broken by rivers
  Average height    900-1600 m                              ~600 m
  Highest peak      Anaimudi (2695 m)                       Mahendragiri (1501 m)

questions.question: Describe the Thar Desert briefly.
questions.answer: The THAR DESERT lies in north-west India (western Rajasthan, parts of Gujarat) and extends into Pakistan. It is hot and arid: annual rainfall less than 150 mm; daytime summer temperatures often exceed 45 °C. Surface features: SAND DUNES (some shifting), rocky outcrops, salt lakes (SAMBHAR, Pachpadra, Didwana). The only large river is the LUNI, which is non-perennial and ends in the Rann of Kachchh. Despite the harsh climate, the Thar has supported pastoral and oasis communities for centuries, and is famous for its forts (Jaisalmer), camel caravans, folk music and textile crafts.

questions.question: Describe the location, geology and importance of the Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep island groups.
questions.answer:
ANDAMAN AND NICOBAR ISLANDS
 - Location: in the BAY OF BENGAL, off the eastern coast.
 - Number: about 572 islands of which only ~38 are inhabited.
 - Geology: mostly VOLCANIC in origin and the southern extension of the Arakan mountains of Myanmar; Barren Island has India's only active volcano.
 - People: indigenous tribes including the Sentinelese, the Onge, the Jarawa and the Great Andamanese.
 - Capital: PORT BLAIR (on South Andaman island).
 - Importance: strategic location near the Strait of Malacca; biodiversity hotspot; tourism (Havelock, Neil islands); tropical evergreen forests.

LAKSHADWEEP
 - Location: in the ARABIAN SEA, about 200-400 km off the Kerala coast.
 - Number: 36 small CORAL islands and reefs; only 10 inhabited.
 - Geology: ATOLLS — coral islands built up on submerged volcanic peaks.
 - Capital: KAVARATTI.
 - Importance: rich marine biodiversity; tuna fisheries; tourism; vulnerable to sea-level rise from climate change.

questions.question: The capital of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands is ____.
The capital of Lakshadweep is ____.
Name India's neighbouring countries.
questions.answer: Seven land neighbours: PAKISTAN (north-west), AFGHANISTAN (across Pakistan-occupied Kashmir), CHINA (north), NEPAL and BHUTAN (north), BANGLADESH and MYANMAR (east). Across the sea: SRI LANKA (to the south) and MALDIVES (to the south-west).

questions.question: What are the four longitudinal regions of the Himalayas?
questions.answer: From west to east: (1) PUNJAB Himalaya (Indus to Sutlej — also called Kashmir Himalaya); (2) KUMAON Himalaya (Sutlej to Kali — in Uttarakhand); (3) NEPAL Himalaya (Kali to Tista — mostly in Nepal, with India's Sikkim portion); (4) ASSAM Himalaya (Tista to Brahmaputra — in Sikkim, Bhutan, Arunachal Pradesh).

questions.question: Identify the three regional divisions of the Northern Plains.
questions.answer: (1) PUNJAB-HARYANA plain — in the west, drained by tributaries of the Indus (Beas, Sutlej, Ravi). (2) GANGA plain — the largest, stretching from Delhi/Haryana east through UP, Bihar, Jharkhand into West Bengal; drained by the Ganga and its tributaries. (3) BRAHMAPUTRA valley — in Assam in the north-east; a narrow valley between the Eastern Himalayas and the Meghalaya plateau, drained by the Brahmaputra.

questions.question: What are the two main divisions of the Peninsular Plateau?
questions.answer:
(1) CENTRAL HIGHLANDS — north of the Narmada river. Includes the Aravalli range (north-west), the Vindhya range, the Satpura range, and the Malwa and Chhota Nagpur plateaus.
(2) DECCAN PLATEAU — south of the Narmada. Bordered by the Western Ghats and Eastern Ghats; covered in places by the Deccan Traps lava.

questions.question: Why do the Western Ghats receive much more rainfall than the Eastern Ghats?
questions.answer: Because of the SOUTH-WEST MONSOON winds. These winds blow from the Arabian Sea towards the land. The Western Ghats, lying parallel to the west coast, force the moist monsoon winds to RISE; as they rise, they cool and release their moisture as ORONOGRAPHIC RAINFALL on the windward (western) slopes. By the time the winds reach the Eastern Ghats, they have already lost most of their moisture, leaving the eastern slopes in a RAIN-SHADOW. This is why the west coast (Konkan, Goa, Malabar) gets >2000 mm a year while the Deccan interior often gets <800 mm. The Eastern Ghats themselves get more rain from the NORTH-EAST monsoon in winter, but overall much less.

questions.question: Describe the climate and life of the Thar Desert.
questions.answer: CLIMATE: arid; annual rainfall less than 150 mm; daytime summer temperatures often above 45 °C, winter nights can drop near freezing. Sand-laden hot winds (loo) are common in summer. SURFACE: shifting sand dunes, rocky outcrops, salt lakes (Sambhar, Pachpadra). VEGETATION: thorny scrub, khejri trees, cacti. WATER: scarce; the Luni is the only large river but is seasonal. LIFE: people depend on PASTORALISM (camels, sheep, goats) and limited oasis-style agriculture (millets, bajra). The Indira Gandhi Canal has brought Sutlej water and transformed parts of the desert into farmland. Famous for forts (Jaisalmer), folk music, textiles and the Pushkar fair.

questions.question: Why does the Eastern Coastal Plain have broad deltas while the Western Coastal Plain does not?
questions.answer:
Because the major peninsular rivers — the MAHANADI, GODAVARI, KRISHNA and KAVERI — flow EASTWARD into the Bay of Bengal. As they reach the sea they slow down and deposit huge quantities of silt, building broad deltas (the Godavari-Krishna delta is the largest). This makes the eastern coastal plain wide (~100-130 km) and very fertile.

Western peninsular rivers either flow into the Arabian Sea via small estuaries (Narmada, Tapti) or are short and steep, dropping straight off the Western Ghats with no space to build deltas. Hence the WESTERN coastal plain is narrow (~50-100 km) and has no major deltas — but does have excellent natural HARBOURS (Mumbai, Kochi, Mangalore).

questions.question: Why are the Himalayas important to India?
questions.answer:
Several reasons:
(1) NATURAL BARRIER — they have historically protected India from invasions and from the cold winds of Central Asia.
(2) CLIMATIC EFFECT — they block the monsoon winds and force them to rain over India; they also block the cold Siberian winds, keeping India warmer than countries at similar latitudes.
(3) SOURCE OF RIVERS — perennial rivers (Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra and their tributaries) rise in Himalayan glaciers, supporting Indian agriculture and water needs year-round.
(4) BIODIVERSITY — many endemic plants and animals.
(5) MINERALS AND FORESTS — timber, medicinal plants, some minerals.
(6) HYDROELECTRIC POTENTIAL — fast-flowing Himalayan streams can generate vast power.
(7) TOURISM — pilgrimage sites (Char Dham, Amarnath, Vaishno Devi) and hill stations.
(8) CULTURAL — distinct Himalayan communities and traditions.

questions.question: What are the minerals found in the Peninsular Plateau?
questions.answer:
The Peninsular Plateau is India's richest mineral region. Major minerals include:
 - IRON ORE — in Singhbhum (Jharkhand), Keonjhar (Odisha), Bellary (Karnataka), Goa.
 - COAL — in the Damodar valley (Jharia, Bokaro, Raniganj — Jharkhand and West Bengal).
 - MANGANESE — Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha.
 - BAUXITE (aluminium ore) — Odisha, Jharkhand, Maharashtra.
 - COPPER — Singhbhum, Khetri (Rajasthan).
 - MICA — Bihar, Jharkhand, Rajasthan.
 - LIMESTONE — Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh.
The abundance of these minerals has made the plateau the heartland of India's heavy industry — iron and steel (Jamshedpur, Bhilai, Rourkela), cement, aluminium and metallurgical industries.

questions.question: Write a detailed note on the Peninsular Plateau.
questions.answer:
The Peninsular Plateau is the great triangular plateau of southern India, one of the OLDEST landmasses on Earth — over 3000 million years old in places. It is made of hard PRE-CAMBRIAN igneous and metamorphic rocks (granite, gneiss, basalt) and forms the stable nucleus of the Indian peninsula.

LOCATION AND EXTENT: Bordered in the north by the Aravalli and Rajmahal hills, in the west by the Western Ghats, in the east by the Eastern Ghats, and in the south by the southern tip of India at Kanyakumari. Average elevation: 600-900 m. Total area: about 16 lakh sq km — about half of India.

DIVISIONS:
 - CENTRAL HIGHLANDS (north of the Narmada) — Aravalli, Vindhya, Satpura ranges; Malwa, Chhota Nagpur, Meghalaya plateaus.
 - DECCAN PLATEAU (south of the Narmada) — the great southern tableland.

MOUNTAIN BORDERS:
 - WESTERN GHATS (Sahyadri) — continuous, 900-1600 m, contain Anaimudi (2695 m). Block south-west monsoon winds.
 - EASTERN GHATS — discontinuous, ~600 m, broken by the great east-flowing rivers.
 - The two meet at the NILGIRI hills in the south.

DECCAN TRAPS: vast layers of basaltic lava erupted ~65 million years ago, now forming black regur soil over much of western Deccan — excellent for cotton cultivation.

RIVERS: most great peninsular rivers flow east to the Bay of Bengal — Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri. The Narmada and Tapti are exceptions, flowing west to the Arabian Sea through rift valleys.

MINERAL WEALTH: iron, coal, manganese, bauxite, copper, mica — making it India's industrial heartland (Jamshedpur, Bhilai, Bokaro).

IMPORTANCE: agricultural (cotton, oilseeds, sugarcane), mineral-and-industrial, water-resource (huge hydro projects on the Narmada, Krishna, Godavari), and historical (Maurya, Vijayanagara, Mughal, Maratha kingdoms).
